b002: The site for a fashion label whose whole identity is anti-luxury luxury. It should feel harsh and confrontational on a large screen, and still function as an e-commerce interface.
b013: Packaging for a Greek olive oil sold at a premium price. The label carries origin data, acidity figures and harvest dates in Greek and English inside a 40mm strip, so we need a condensed cut and tabular figures. It is screen printed onto glass, which loses detail below 6pt, so nothing delicate. It should read as precise and provenance-obsessed.
b023: A printed provenance dossier accompanying a Greek antiquities dealer's catalogue, in Greek and English at 10pt. Polytonic Greek is needed for the inscriptions. Footnoting is heavy with superscript references, so the face needs real superior figures rather than scaled ones, plus small caps and tabular figures for the measurement tables. Dry and exacting.
b024: A deck presenting a jewellery house to Russian retail partners. Cyrillic headlines at 50px, body at 18px, projected and also sent as a PDF. We need Cyrillic drawn to the same standard as the Latin, at least a light and a regular with true italics, old-style figures for prose and lining figures for the price tables. It has to feel expensive and quiet.
b026: Packaging for a Japanese single-origin whisky sold internationally. The back label sets Japanese and English at 6pt in a fixed area, including cask numbers and ABV, so we need a condensed cut with tabular figures and a Latin that pairs with the Japanese without a weight mismatch. It prints on textured paper. Precise and understated.
b028: A deck presenting a playful Russian accessories brand to buyers, and it should feel light and confident.
b050: A printed lookbook for a cashmere brand. It should feel warm and tactile rather than cold and editorial, and the captions run small alongside large photography.
b054: The e-commerce site for a Vietnamese silk house. It needs to feel refined, and the Vietnamese product descriptions must sit as elegantly on the page as the English ones.
b056: Packaging for a Japanese tea brand entering Western markets. The box carries Japanese and English together, and it should feel warm and handmade rather than corporate.
b071: A printed brand history for a Vietnamese jeweller that should feel established.
b077: A shopping app for a Vietnamese luxury department store that should feel upmarket.
b099: A deck presenting a European luxury group's results to Japanese partners, in Japanese and English. Headlines at 44px and dense financial tables at 14px, so tabular lining figures are essential and the Latin has to match the Japanese in weight. We need five weights and a licence permitting embedding in distributed PDFs. Formal and unmistakably corporate.
b103: A loyalty app for a Russian department store that should feel welcoming.
b118: The site for a Russian artisan ceramics brand. Body at 17px in Russian and English, product stories run long so it has to stay comfortable, Cyrillic italics for the maker quotes, and at least three weights. Prices and dimensions appear throughout, so tabular figures are needed. Warm and handmade without being twee.
b126: A printed catalogue for a Vietnamese streetwear label. It is bilingual, and it should feel energetic and irreverent while the garment specifications stay readable at small sizes.
b152: The website of a Greek high jewellery house that should feel authoritative and old.
b153: A mobile app for a Japanese luxury hotel group, in Japanese and English. It has to feel formal and reassuring, and the Latin should not look lightweight beside the Japanese.
b155: A shopping app for a label built on deliberate ugliness. Type must be aggressive at 15px body and 32px headings, needs an extreme heavy weight and a very tight condensed cut, and has to stay WCAG AA legible despite the harshness. Tabular figures for prices. The face should feel like it is shouting.
b172: A printed campaign booklet for a Greek avant-garde fashion label that should feel confrontational.
b178: A long-form printed brand book for a colourful accessories label. It reads for extended stretches so it has to stay comfortable, and the personality needs to survive being set at text sizes.
b193: A printed invitation suite for a Russian couture house that should feel exquisite.
b006: A national tax filing portal. Forms carry dense field labels at 14px and monetary values that must align, so tabular figures are required. WCAG AA minimum, ideally AAA for body text. We need unambiguous 1, l and I for reference codes, at least four weights, and a licence permitting self-hosting on government infrastructure. Neutral and unmistakably clear.
b021: A Greek parliamentary committee report, roughly 400 pages at 10pt in Greek and English. Footnoting is heavy and clauses are numbered, so we need superior figures, tabular figures for the budget annexes, and Greek with correct tonos in both roman and italic. It must read as official and be free to redistribute.
b041: A Japanese municipal planning document that should read as official.
b047: Packaging for a public health kit distributed in Russian-speaking regions. Instructions set at 8pt in Russian and English inside a fixed area, so we need a condensed cut with Cyrillic that stays clear at that size. It should feel reassuring rather than bureaucratic, must survive printing on recycled board, and the licence has to allow government redistribution.
b063: A deck for a Greek ministry announcing a policy programme that should feel official.
b064: Packaging for a national museum's membership card that should feel refined.
b072: Packaging for a Russian state postal service's commemorative stamp collection. It should feel dignified and a little ceremonial, and the Cyrillic titling is the main design element.
b076: A deck for a Vietnamese disaster preparedness campaign, presented in Vietnamese. Headlines at 52px have to feel urgent and unavoidable, body at 20px has to stay readable in poorly lit community halls. Vietnamese diacritics must not clip at heading sizes. We need an extreme heavy weight, and the licence must permit unrestricted government use.
b078: Packaging for a Japanese emergency supply kit that should feel urgent.
b085: A Japanese building code manual, 600 pages at 9pt in Japanese with English terminology. The Latin has to pair with a Japanese Gothic face at matched weight, hold up at that size in three columns, and provide tabular figures for the load tables. We need a monospace companion for code references and a licence permitting redistribution.
b096: An emergency alert app for a Russian-speaking region that should feel urgent.
b098: A Russian-language guide to social benefits, read by people who find the system intimidating. It runs long so it has to stay comfortable, and the tone should feel human rather than official.
b116: A Greek city council site encouraging young people to use public libraries. It is bilingual, and it should feel inviting rather than municipal while staying accessible.
b127: A deck presenting infrastructure statistics to a Vietnamese provincial authority. It is dense with figures that need to align, and it should read as impartial and technical.
b132: A Japanese city's app for reporting street maintenance problems. It should feel approachable enough that people actually use it, and the Latin should sit comfortably beside the Japanese labels.
b135: A Vietnamese national identity document booklet. Text sets at 7pt in a fixed area in Vietnamese and English, printed by intaglio, so strokes cannot be too fine and the diacritics must stay distinct at that size. We need tabular figures for numbers and dates, a licence permitting sovereign use, and a face with no stylistic personality at all.
b150: A printed programme for a state ceremonial occasion that should feel formal and beautiful.
b151: A city app encouraging household recycling. Type must work at 14px for instructions and 28px for section headings, needs five weights, and has to stay WCAG AA compliant while feeling friendly. Icons sit alongside labels, so a slightly rounded character helps, though it must not become childish. The licence must permit municipal use.
b170: A Vietnamese government site for new parents registering a birth that should feel supportive.
b171: A Greek public inquiry report into an industrial disaster. It runs long and has to stay readable, but the tone should be unsparing rather than diplomatic.
b207: A printed statistical yearbook from a national statistics office. It is almost entirely tables, so figures must align perfectly and stay legible at small sizes, and it should read as neutral.
